newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO tells Moslem refugees to quit contested village.
newsitem.headline: NATO tells Moslem refugees to quit contested village.

text.p: A U.S. general said on Wednesday that Moslem refugees reoccupying a devastated village on Bosnian Serb territory had violated the Dayton peace accord.

NATO peacekeepers want them to leave and apply for permission to return to their former homes, but the refugees have refused to budge, raising tensions in the area despite appeals for reason by Bosnian Prime Minister Hasan Muratovic.
A major dispute loomed after about 100 Moslems, some armed, entered Jusici, east of Tuzla, last Friday. They include pre-war residents of the village driven from their homes by fighting.

"They (the Moslems) directly violated the (Dayton peace) treaty by coming here with arms," U.S. General George Casey, whose troops patrol the area together with Russian soldiers, told reporters on Wednesday.

"This group must leave and process the papers to come back in according to the policies laid down by Dayton and the UNHCR (U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees). That is the position of the international community," he said.

The NATO spokesman in Sarajevo, Major Brett Boudreau, said earlier that the goal was to get Bosnian Moslem and Serb authorities to agree to a six-point U.N. process governing a phased and orderly resettlement of villages such as Jusici.
Mostly destroyed in the 43-month Bosnian war, Jusici sits inside Serb-held territory and within a demilitarised "zone of separation" patrolled by NATO forces.

A member of the International Police Task Force (IPTF), monitoring post-war Bosnia, told Reuters the situation in Jusici seemed more tense on Wednesday, after a 48-hour Serb deadline for the withdrawal expired.

"It appears that some of the Moslem people are trying to taunt the Serb police in the area...maybe venturing out of the village a little too far for the liking of the Serb police," Thomas Hickox, IPTF commander in nearby Sapna said.
U.N. sources reported that the number of Moslems in the village had risen to 300 and a Reuters reporter said it appeared more women and children had turned up.
Serb Minister of the Interior Dragan Kijac said the Moslems still had weapons hidden away and warned he would restore Serb authority over the village.
"I assure you that citizens who crossed from the Federation still possess weapons hidden after they crossed, or hidden earlier in various places," he told Serb television.
"All these reasons, as well as my obligations by law, force me to take measures to establish the authority of Republika Srpska in these areas," he said.
He did not specify what measures he would take or when. His statement came hours after the ITPF praised his restraint.
Prime Minister Muratovic visited the village on Wednesday to try to defuse the tension.

"I came to appeal to you to show that we're a civilised people, that we only want our rights and that we'll fight for them in the most civilised way," he told the crowd gathered in and around a house in the centre of the village.
"First we have to see if you can live here at all," Muratovic said, alluding to devastated houses, lack of running water and electricity in the village and the impending winter.
"Yes, yes, we can live here," members of the crowd shouted.

International officials have sought since Friday to defuse the situation, with little apparent progress. NATO troops earlier seized and destroyed weapons from the Moslems and have urged Serb authorities not to enter the village.
Serb authorities insist the Moslems withdraw and register to re-enter the village according to guidelines which were drawn up by the United Nations.
